lead: Berthe Marie Pauline Morisot was a French painter, printmaker and a member of the circle of painters in Paris who became known as the Impressionists.
paras: Morisot painted the light of rooms and gardens in fast, feathery strokes, and her pictures are dominated by white. She was one of the founding members of the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, and her handling is among the loosest of the group.
The chapters below follow her from copying in the Louvre to the white interiors of her married years, and end with what our archive shows.

chapters.title: Copyist and student of Corot
chapters.text:
Morisot was born in Bourges in 1841 and grew up in Paris. She and her sister Edma studied with private teachers and then with the landscapist Camille Corot, and copied in the Louvre. She exhibited at the official Salon from 1864.

The early landscapes are the work of a Corot student, in quiet {{Sage}}, {{Dove Grey}} and {{Olive}} greens, with soft light on water and a low horizon.

The interest is in the thin, silvery handling, which stays all her life. She left areas of canvas lightly covered, so that the ground shows through as a pale tone.

chapters.title: Manet and the model
chapters.text:
She met Edouard Manet in 1868 and sat for him several times, among them the dark-toned Repose of 1870 and the portrait with a bunch of violets. Their exchange ran both ways. He loosened his strokes, and she made more use of black and strong tone contrast, by the usual account.

In 1874 she married his brother Eugène, and in the same year showed at the first Impressionist exhibition, where she was the only woman among the thirty participants listed by most accounts.

The Cradle, from 1872, is the key picture of these years. A veil of white muslin covers the baby, and the whole canvas is built from tones close to {{Ivory}}, {{Pearl}} and {{Blush}}.

The Cradle depicts her sister Edma and her niece. It was among the pictures shown in 1874, and critics of the time found it unfinished, because the brush marks are visible and the edges soft.

chapters.title: White rooms and gardens
chapters.text:
In the late 1870s and 1880s she painted her daughter Julie, born in 1878, her family, and women in gardens. The brushwork grows looser and the color lighter, and there is often more canvas showing than paint.

The whites are not plain. She modulated them with {{Powder Blue}}, {{Lavender}} and {{Peach}}, and used a green accent such as {{Mint}} near a pale dress to bring out its warmth.

What to look for in the real pictures is the way a white dress is made with separate strokes of near-colors, and how the edge between dress and background is not drawn but suggested.

She often worked in pastel and watercolor as well as oil, and the same pale tone runs through all of them. Look for a ring of pale canvas around a figure, where she simply stopped.
chapters.pull: Morisot's whites are never one white: they are modulated with blue, lavender and peach.

chapters.title: Late work and what our archive shows
chapters.text:
In her last decade she drew more, and the lines of her compositions are visible under the paint. She died in 1895, aged fifty-four.

Our archive holds 420 of her paintings. In the pale areas {{Greyish White}} leads, at about eight per cent, with Linen grey and {{Olive-Buff}} close behind. Her darkest large areas are Smoky Black, but only at about nine per cent.

She uses Bistre, Smoky Black and Dark olive brown less than other painters of her years do, in some cases by a large factor. That fits a painter who kept even her shadows light. These are photographs, and a canvas left thin photographs lighter than a thick one.

Her daughter Julie later helped to look after the studio and her records, and her pictures of Julie from childhood to young adulthood form one of the longest portrait series by an Impressionist.
